html:
Recent advances in neuroscience have fundamentally transformed our understanding of glial cells from passive support elements to active computational partners in neural information processing. They make up a substantial fraction of brain cells (on par with neurons in number) and carry out diverse roles that extend well beyond basic support. In fact, glia are integral to neural information processing: they regulate the extracellular environment, modulate synaptic activity, influence signal propagation, and even participate in learning and memory processes 1, 2 One proposed mechanism links astrocyte signaling and D-serine release to shifts in the threshold for synaptic plasticity (Figure).

Astrocytes

Astrocytes fundamentally reshape our understanding of synaptic processing by forming "tripartite synapses" where they actively participate alongside pre- and postsynaptic neurons. Single astrocytes contact over 100,000 synapses, with their perisynaptic processes covering 50-80% of synaptic surfaces. This extensive coverage enables astrocytes to monitor and modulate neural activity with remarkable precision.

Astrocytes exhibit complex intracellular calcium patterns that integrate information from multiple synaptic inputs and produce nonlinear output responses. These calcium signals operate across multiple timescales: rapid responses (100-500 milliseconds) for immediate synaptic modulation, intermediate responses (1-5 seconds) for network coordination, and slow responses (minutes to hours) for long-term homeostatic regulation 3.

Functions

Astrocytes are the brain’s primary vacuum cleaners for glutamate and other transmitters. High-affinity transporters EAAT1 (GLAST) and EAAT2 (GLT-1) on perisynaptic membranes siphon away >90% of released glutamate in a few milliseconds, preventing excitotoxicity and resetting the cleft. The same transporters, together with astrocytic GATs for GABA and glycine, feed the glutamate/GABA-glutamine cycle: astrocytes convert the captured transmitter to glutamine and shuttle it back to neurons for resynthesis, linking synaptic transmission to nitrogen and carbon metabolism. Disrupting EAAT2 in mice or humans produces seizures and rapid neurodegeneration 4, 5.

Astrocytes are the metabolic quartermasters of active circuits. During bursts of activity they break down their private glycogen stores and export lactate through MCT1/MCT4; neurons import it via MCT2 and oxidize it. This astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle (and the associated glycogenolysis) is now known to be required for hippocampal LTP and long-term memory consolidation in vivo, and it functions as a redox buffer that lets neurons run sparingly on local glucose during high-frequency firing 6, 7 A review illustrates lactate metabolism in the brain (Figure) 22.

Astrocytes sculpt circuits structurally. During development and adult plasticity they secrete thrombospondins, hevin and glypicans that nucleate and mature excitatory synapses, while complement tagging and MEGF10/MERTK signaling drive synapse pruning. Cholinergic or noradrenergic input to astrocytes can massively up-regulate these synaptogenic programs, showing that astrocytes gate experience-dependent wiring rules 8, 9

Astrocytes contribute to synaptic plasticity through metaplasticity mechanisms. They can slide the threshold for long-term potentiation and depression according to the BCM learning rule by releasing D-serine, effectively implementing activity-dependent adjustment of plasticity thresholds 10, 11.

Astrocytes couple with blood vessels to adjust local blood flow, ensuring active neurons get adequate energy supply.

Astrocytes are now recognized as active "rhythm generators" that can both synchronize local circuits and impose brain-wide oscillatory structure

Astrocytes sit at every excitatory and inhibitory synapse, sensing transmitter spill-over with high-gain GPCRs. An incoming burst of neuronal activity triggers intracellular IP3/Ca2+ waves that last hundreds of milliseconds in a single cell, then-through gliotransmitter release (ATP->adenosine, glutamate, D-serine) and rapid K+/water buffering-feed back onto nearby neurons. In hippocampal slices and in vivo, blocking vesicular release from astrocytes or knocking down Ca2+ signaling reduces γ\gamma-power and de-synchronizes interneuron firing; computational work shows that reinstating slow astrocytic modulation instantly restores γ\gamma-coherence across a broad parameter range 12, 13

Because astrocytes are themselves coupled by connexin-43 gap junctions, their Ca2+ events can propagate as regenerative waves spanning hundreds of microns to millimeters ("glissandi") on a time-scale of seconds. These waves ride on top of the neuronal network and entrain ultra-slow (0.01-0.1 Hz) LFP fluctuations, effectively stitching together distant cortical domains [Large-Scale Calcium Waves Traveling through Astrocytic Networks In Vivo; 14]

At the scale of brain states, cortical astrocytes can flip the cortex from a high-frequency, desynchronized mode into the synchronized <1 Hz slow-oscillation that dominates deep sleep. Two-photon Ca2+ imaging combined with optogenetics shows that an astrocytic glutamate transient reliably precedes each down-state, and direct photostimulation of astrocytes is sufficient to trigger the transition in vivo 15

Together these processes knit single-synapse timing (milliseconds) into whole-brain rhythms (seconds to minutes), providing both the scaffolding and the modulatory "clock" that neurons alone cannot supply.

Single-cell atlas work now shows cortex- versus hippocampus-specific astrocyte subtypes with distinct transcriptional and electrophysiological profiles, implying that all of the functions above are locally tuned 16

Oligodendrocytes

Oligodendrocytes wrap myelin sheaths around axons, which dramatically increases the speed of action potential conduction. Individual oligodendrocytes can myelinate up to 100 axonal segments, compared to the 1:1 ratio of peripheral Schwann cells 17. By insulating axons, myelin not only makes long-range communication faster but also synchronizes the timing of neuronal signals across distant circuits 18. Precise timing is crucial for distributed computations (for instance, synchronized inputs can summate effectively at a postsynaptic neuron). Thus, oligodendrocytes indirectly help neurons perform computations that rely on timing (like coincidence detection and oscillatory coordination) by tuning conduction velocities. A 2026 review summarizes activity-dependent myelination (Figure) 21.

The computational significance of oligodendrocytes becomes apparent in their activity-dependent myelination. Motor skill learning, for example, has been shown to increase oligodendrocyte generation by 30-50% in relevant brain regions within 2 weeks 19, demonstrating experience-dependent structural plasticity. This adaptive myelination enables precise timing control with millisecond accuracy, essential for spike-timing-dependent plasticity and proper neural circuit function. A 2026 review relates activity-dependent myelination to circuit function (Figure) 23.

They also support axonal metabolism (supplying nutrients like lactate), which keeps neurons healthy during high-frequency activity. From a systems perspective, myelin plasticity provides a mechanism for the brain to adjust communication latencies and maintain optimal information transmission as networks remodel with learning.

Microglia

Microglia are the brain’s resident immune cells, but they also serve as dynamic regulators of neural circuits. Even in their "resting" surveillance state, microglia constantly extend processes to monitor synaptic health and activity 2.

Microglial processes continuously survey the entire brain parenchyma every 4-6 hours, with individual processes extending and retracting at 1-2 μm/minute 20.

A crucial function they perform is synaptic pruning - identifying and eliminating weaker or excess synapses, especially during development and plasticity periods. This pruning is computationally significant: it refines circuit wiring, removing noise or unused connections, which enhances the efficiency and capacity of neural networks. In the adult brain, microglia also modulate synapses through secreted signaling molecules. For instance, microglia release brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and cytokines that can strengthen or weaken synapses and influence the balance of LTP/LTD 2. This means microglia can adjust the gain of neural connections and even gate memory processes. Furthermore, microglia help maintain homeostasis by clearing debris and releasing anti-inflammatory or repair factors after injury, which indirectly preserves the computational integrity of neural circuits.

In summary, microglia act as adaptive sculptors and maintenance workers for the brain’s networks - ensuring that neuronal ensembles are optimally wired and that synaptic connections are dynamically regulated for learning and memory.
